guide.title: Fenbendazole
guide.description: A veterinary dewormer with mixed cancer-model findings, anecdotal human efficacy reports and documented liver-injury cases.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Cancer benefit: Not established. The selected human efficacy evidence is anecdotal, while the animal studies give mixed results. This page has no controlled human trial establishing tumor response, longer survival or a safe cancer regimen. This describes the evidence reviewed here, not an exhaustive claim about every study that might exist.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: Clinical evidence: Low. A six-patient case series included one prostate-cancer patient who received fenbendazole with ivermectin and chlorine dioxide. The other five cases cannot be counted as fenbendazole cases. With multiple interventions, no control group and retrospective reporting, the reported improvement cannot establish that fenbendazole caused a cancer response. Clinical evidence: Low. In Gao 2008, lymphoma tumors in mice were smaller with fenbendazole plus supplemented vitamins (P = 0.009). Fenbendazole alone did not differ significantly from control (P = 0.12). The combination result cannot be attributed to fenbendazole alone, and nonsignificance does not prove equivalence.

questions.question: What do the animal experiments show?
questions.answer: Clinical evidence: Low. Duan 2012 found no change in EMT6 mouse mammary-tumor growth, invasion, metastasis or response to local radiation with fenbendazole-containing chow. Duan 2013 also found no improvement in tumor growth or radiation response with intensive regimens. Those authors concluded that their experiments provided no evidence of value in cancer therapy; these findings apply to the tested models, not every possible cancer or regimen.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Safety evidence: Low for estimating frequency or individual risk. A 2024 case report described biopsy-confirmed severe liver injury after self-administration, with liver tests returning to normal after cessation. This is a serious human safety signal, but a case report cannot estimate how often it occurs.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: Human contraindication guidance: Not established by these studies. The human liver-injury reports identify harm after self-administration, but do not define a validated list of contraindications or a group in whom fenbendazole is safe.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: Safety evidence: Low. A patient receiving nivolumab/relatlimab developed severe liver injury after increasing self-administered fenbendazole. The report distinguished suspected drug injury from immune-mediated hepatitis. It does not establish the size or mechanism of an interaction, or provide a safe combination schedule.

sections.label: Dosing
sections.paragraph: Human cancer dose: Not established. The cited cell and mouse studies do not establish a dose, treatment duration or monitoring schedule for people. The human combination case is not a dose-finding study, and the liver-injury reports do not define a safe threshold.

sections.label: Results
sections.paragraph: Clinical evidence: Low. Dogra 2018 reported slower A549 lung-cancer xenograft growth in mice. This positive result is specific to that model and regimen, and cannot establish benefit in people or across cancers.

sections.label: Quality
sections.paragraph: Official context: The cited FDA approval concerns an animal oral suspension and its labeled species. It does not assess veterinary products as human cancer medicines.

sections.label: Status
sections.paragraph: Official context: In January 2026, the FDA approved a generic fenbendazole oral suspension for specified parasite infections in cattle and goats. That animal-product approval does not establish approval, efficacy or a dose for human cancer treatment.

summary.text: Clinical evidence: Low. In lung-cancer models, fenbendazole partly disrupted microtubules, interfered with cell division and increased cell death. These laboratory findings explain a research hypothesis; they do not show that an effective exposure can be reached safely in people.

questions.title: Are p53 and glucose effects consistent?
questions.text: Clinical evidence: Low. Dogra reported p53 activation and reduced glucose uptake in lung-cancer cells. The pathway is not consistent across models: Park found no change in glucose consumption or lactate production in H4IIE rat liver-cancer cells, and a separate colorectal-cell abstract reported effects that did not require p53.

questions.title: Does fenbendazole target Hedgehog or cholesterol transport?
questions.text: Hedgehog or NPC1 cholesterol-transport mechanism: Not established for fenbendazole in the evidence reviewed here. The cited fenbendazole experiments test microtubules, cell stress, p53 and metabolic effects; they do not demonstrate a Hedgehog or NPC1-mediated anticancer effect. Findings for a different drug cannot supply that missing evidence.
